tweets.text:
Open interest is just a number. What matters is who owns it.
 
10,000 contracts owned by one institution that always rolls is a pin you can lean on. They behave predictably, the strike behaves predictably, the vol surface around it tells you when they're about to move. There is a footprint on the surface consistent with the trade and the positioning of dealers the other side.

The JPMorgan put spread collar that rolls every quarter? Whole street knows the timing. Vol front-runs it. That's a tradeable pattern.
 
However, same 10,000 contracts scattered across 200 retail accounts, that's noise. 

Some exercise late, some don't exercise at all, some get assigned by accident. The strike behaves randomly.
 
This is why dividend trades, expiry pins, and strike-magnet patterns work better in stocks with concentrated institutional flow than in retail favourites.
 
Which are your favourite names that have predictable flows?

tweets.text:
The S&P dropped about 2% last week. Doesn't sound like much.

But look at what the vol surface did. 5-delta puts gained over 10 vol points. The term structure inverted. Skew blew out to levels you normally only see during genuine panic.

The vol surface was pricing a crash while the index chart looked like a garden-variety pullback.

This is typical. Vol sees the stress building in positioning and flows before it shows up in spot. Dealers are getting hit with put demand. Hedgers are scrambling. The footprint is all over the surface if you know where to look.

Instead of staring at candlestick charts waiting for confirmation. Reading the vol surface gives you more information about how risk is being priced beyond the spot level.

TLDR: Crash risk went up. Bigtime!
